analysis.one_liner: Prioritizes bondholders, military pay, Social Security, and Medicare if the debt limit blocks other federal payments.
analysis.headline: The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar in October 2015, but no committee ever acted on it and it never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: If the government hits its legal borrowing cap and cannot pay all of its bills, this bill sets an order: bondholders get paid first, then active-duty military pay, Social Security, and Medicare. Everything else the government owes — from federal salaries and contractor payments to veterans' benefits and food assistance — would come last and could go unpaid. The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar but never advanced to any committee or floor vote, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the clearest winner would be holders of U.S. Treasury debt — banks, money market funds, foreign governments, and wealthy investors — who would be first in line for payment in a default. Social Security recipients, Medicare beneficiaries, and active-duty service members would also be protected, while everyone else owed money by the federal government would bear the risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bondholders, plus Social Security and Medicare recipients

how_it_helps.text: If the debt ceiling is hit, Social Security and Medicare payments would continue rather than be delayed or skipped.
Active-duty military pay would be protected, so service members would keep receiving compensation during a default.
Bondholders would be paid first, which backers argue prevents the most damaging consequence of a default: a collapse in confidence in U.S. debt.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone owed money by the federal government outside the four protected categories: federal employees, military retirees and veterans, government contractors, doctors billing Medicare-adjacent programs, and other benefit recipients, who would absorb the shortfall if the debt limit were hit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal workers, contractors, and other beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: The bill puts bondholders first: principal and interest on debt held by the public is priority number one, ahead of every other government obligation.

If the debt limit is hit, the plan leaves all other legal obligations — federal salaries, military retirees, veterans' benefits, tax refunds, payments to doctors outside Medicare, contracts, and other benefit programs — unprotected and first in line for cuts or delays.

The Treasury and many legal experts have long argued that picking and choosing among payments after the debt limit is hit may not be technically or legally feasible; the bill attempts to solve that by statute rather than addressing the underlying constraint.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: As a contingency plan, prioritizing Social Security and military pay is broadly popular, but the bill's first priority is bondholders, and paying them while skipping other legal obligations is legally doubtful and untested. The deeper tradeoff: a default-prevention plan aimed only at protecting creditors and major benefit checks can make brinkmanship easier to repeat, and it offers nothing to the retirees, contractors, and families who would face missed payments anyway.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee took it up and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the Default Prevention Act on October 19, 2015, during a period of recurring fights over raising the federal debt limit.
No senators signed on as cosponsors.
The bill was read a second time on October 20, 2015, and placed on the Senate Calendar of General Orders (Calendar No. 273) — the last action ever taken on it.
No committee held a hearing or markup, and the Senate never voted on the bill before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bondholders and other creditors to the federal government are better off that this version died, because it would have made them the first claim on any default-scenario payments; no one else gained anything from the bill dying, since it never took effect either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bondholders protected from an untested default plan

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was placed on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split on its merits is on the record.

industries.industry: Holders of U.S. Treasury debt (banks, foreign governments, money market funds, bond investors)
industries.note: The bill's first-listed priority is paying principal and interest on debt held by the public before any other obligation, making creditors the most protected class in a default. That protection would primarily benefit large financial institutions and wealthy households that hold the most Treasuries.
Medicare payments would continue during a default, keeping hospitals and doctors paid for seniors' care. Providers outside the Medicare program get no such protection.
Payments under federal contracts and civilian paychecks are not on the priority list, so they would absorb the brunt of any default under this plan.
